title: collector-backpressure-and-queryable-archive-guidance
content:
Purpose:
This note captures design guidance and an operational playbook for collector backpressure handling and the implementation of a queryable evidence archive that sits downstream of the collection layer. It focuses on pragmatic heuristics for retention, tiering exported SIEM payloads, and how RBAC v2 controls should shape access to both live pipelines and archived evidence. The target audience is infra engineers, security platform owners, and SREs managing evidence pipelines.

Motivation / Problems we solve:
- Collectors ingest telemetry at variable bursts (ingress storms, tenant replays). Left unchecked this trips durable queues and delays alerts.
- Long-term evidence must be searchable for audits but should not retain hot-format copies forever.
- RBAC rules and export pipelines (SIEM exporters, evidence-forensics API) must be auditable and least-privilege.
- SIEM exports need consistent mapping and graceful degradation when downstream systems are rate-limited.

Scope and non-goals:
- Scope: collector backpressure strategies, short->warm->cold archive tiering, queryable archive format decisions, SIEM export fallbacks, RBAC integration points.
- Non-goals: full SIEM connector implementations, encryption-at-rest spec (platform-wide), or per-customer legal retention policy formulation.

High-level architecture (conceptual):
- Ingest collectors (edge agents / sidecars) -> local buffer (ring or on-disk) -> brokered queueing layer (Kafka / Kinesis / SQS) -> processing workers (normalization, pseudonymization) -> evidence store (hot store for 7d) -> queryable archive (cold store with index shards) -> SIEM/export adapters.
- Backpressure control points: collector local buffer, broker-level throttles, worker concurrency autoscaler, adaptive sampler.

Key design guidance:
1) Backpressure strategy (principles):
   - Fast fail upstream: prefer shedding non-essential telemetry early (debug traces, low-value metrics) rather than blocking control-plane evidence like auth events.
   - Classify events by evidence-criticality at ingestion (critical, important, best-effort). Use small event headers inserted by the collector indicating classification.
   - Implement multi-tier backpressure: local buffer drop policy -> broker quota enforcement -> worker-level slow down with token-bucket.
   - Prefer sampling for best-effort tiers with adaptive sampling rate influenced by downstream queue length and SLOs.

2) Collector-level controls:
   - Local persistent queue cap: default 128MB per collector instance; configurable per-customer.
   - Drop policy: LRU by event age for best-effort; reject duplicates heuristically for noisy streams.
   - Emergency mode: when broker latency crosses 5s p50 and queue fullness > 80%, flip to emergency policy where only critical events are persisted and an event-level "skipped_count" counter is emitted for later auditing.
   - Metrics to expose: local_queue_depth, local_disk_usage, dropped_events_total{reason}, emit_rate, classification_distribution.

3) Broker & processing layer heuristics:
   - Broker quotas per-tenant with burst allowance and sustained budget. Enforce with token buckets and expose throttled_tenant_id metrics.
   - Worker concurrency should back off based on processing latency percentiles and disk-backed spill.
   - For catastrophic backpressure (broker unavailable), pipeline must pivot to a spill-to-object-store mode with a compact envelope format (see Archive format).

4) Queryable archive format and tiering:
   - Tier naming: hot (0–7 days), warm (7–90 days), cold (90–365 days), archived (>365 days) — defaults; legal/enterprise customers override.
   - Storage targets: hot -> SSD-backed evidence DB with tokenized index; warm -> compressed columnar store with per-day index shards (Parquet with bloom indices); cold -> compressed object storage with precomputed inverted index shards; archived -> deep archival blob (glacier-style).
   - Envelope format (compact): minimal JSON lines with these top-level fields: event_id, ts_utc, tenant_id, classification, schema_version, normalized_payload_ref (pointer to normalized object or inline small payload), provenance_meta (collector_id, version, sha256). Keep schema_version as a string.
   - Indexing: index tenant_id, ts_utc, event_type, user_id (pseudonymized id), and a small set of EAV-like keys for common lookup. Store per-shard bloom filters for quick membership tests.
   - Query path: queries against archive should first consult bloom index and metadata catalog, then fetch shard ranges and run a projection to return compact results.

5) Retention heuristics and TTL management:
   - Default TTL rules: critical events: 3y, important: 1y, best-effort: 90d. Admin UI override per-tenant and per-evidence-class.
   - Soft-delete model: when TTL expires, mark entries soft_deleted and remove from active index; physically delete during monthly compaction windows. Keep a short grace window (30d) for accidental restores; preserve a deletion_audit record.
   - Retention policy enforcement: central retention service periodically reconciles catalog and triggers compaction jobs. Compaction jobs emit manifests used for compliance reports.

6) SIEM export mapping & graceful degradation:
   - SIEM adapter responsibilities: map canonical envelope to SIEM schema (CEF/LEEF or Splunk HEC), batch and compress, honor upstream classification to choose export priority.
   - Export batching: keep batch windows small for critical events (max 1s or 50 events) and larger for best-effort (5–30s). 
   - Rate-limit awareness: adapters must support backoff with jitter and queue-to-disk spill. If SIEM returns 429 or transient errors, adapters: (1) switch to reduced batch size, (2) reduce export rate proportional to error ratio, (3) escalate to operator alert if >2 minutes of persistent errors.
   - Export fallback: if adapter cannot export for >10 minutes, create a compact export_delta manifest in the archive and flag for re-export job. Do not keep unbounded memory queues.

7) RBAC v2 integration and control plane considerations:
   - Principle: evidence access and export capabilities must be governed by RBAC v2 and logged as first-class events.
   - Role templates: evidence-reader, evidence-exporter, evidence-admin, evidence-auditor. Each role maps to allowed actions (read live/archived, trigger re-export, change retention, view manifests).
   - Audit hooks: every RBAC grant/revoke and every export operation must emit an immutable control-event to the evidence pipeline tagged as control-plane. Control-plane evidence is treated as critical.
   - Time-limited grants: support short-lived export tokens (scoped) for incident responders; require justification field recorded in the control-event.

8) Operational playbook (runbook snippets):
   - Detection: alert on broker_queue_ratio > 0.8 for >2m, local_queue_depth > 75% on >5% of collectors, or SIEM_export_error_rate > 0.05.
   - Triage steps: 1) confirm scope (tenant-wide vs system-wide) 2) check retention/compaction jobs 3) check exporter responses and backoff thresholds 4) flip emergency mode if needed 5) plan re-export (use manifests).
   - Re-export flow: generate re-export manifest from archive for time window and tenant -> spin up re-export job with concurrency cap -> monitor exported_count and error_rate -> mark manifest status.

9) Failure modes and mitigations:
   - Collector restarts churning local disk: ensure local queue has exponential backoff writer and compact checkpoints to avoid re-sending duplicates.
   - Broker partition loss: automatic spill-to-object-store mode + operator page to rebuild partitions from manifests.
   - Silent loss during high sampling: emit periodic sampling_audit events (counts per classification) so auditors can reconstruct approximate event counts.

10) Compliance reporting and evidence provenance:
   - Compaction/manifests must include canonical proof: manifest_id, creator, time_range, shard_list, checksums. Store manifest in immutable store with retention >= longest evidence TTL + 1 year.
   - Provide tooling to produce a compliance bundle: manifests + subset of events + RBAC audit trail for an auditor. Support signed manifests (KMS).

Open questions / tradeoffs to resolve:
- Inline normalized payloads vs pointer: inline improves atomicity but increases archive size; pointers require retention coherence between normalized store and archive.
- Bloom filter false-positive budget vs index size for older cold shards.
- How granular are tenant quotas for spike protection (per-org, per-team, per-dataset)?

Next steps / action items:
- Engineering: prototype spill-to-objstore mode with compact envelope and manifest generation (owner: Daniel Kim, ticket: JIRA-SC-987).
- Security: provide RBAC v2 role templates and emergency-scoped token design (owner: Sofia Martinez).
- SRE: create alert runbook and sample dashboards for backpressure metrics (owner: Asha Patel).
- Compliance: draft compliance bundle generator and manifest signing spec.

Appendix: quick example envelope (compact representation):
{ event_id: "evt_20251104_0001", ts_utc: "2025-11-04T17:23:11Z", tenant_id: "org-42", classification: "critical", schema_version: "v1", normalized_payload_ref: "/normalized/2025-11-04/evt_20251104_0001.json.gz", provenance_meta: "collector=coll-sidecar-1;ver=2.3.1;sha=abc123" }
